newsitem.title: GERMANY: FOCUS-EU vows no new taxes on Internet commerce.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-EU vows no new taxes on Internet commerce.

text.p: A European Union-sponsored conference on Internet commerce agreed in principle on Tuesday there would be no new trade barriers or taxes imposed on companies or individuals wishing to do business in cyberspace.

But the conference, attended by 40 government ministers from Europe, the United States, Japan and Canada, appeared to make little progress on how to regulate encryption technology needed for transaction security on the Internet.

The ministers agreed Internet regulation should be led by private enterprise rather than governments and embraced some ideas proposed by U.S. President Bill Clinton last week, but stopped short of advocating the U.S. proposal in full.
"We have agreed there should be no discriminatory taxes and laws placed on the Internet," said German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt, host of the two-day conference.
"The ministers have agreed that there should only be state regulation where absolutely necessary and private initiative and market forces should have as much room as possible."
The ministers vowed to make a joint effort to clamp down on tax evasion on business deals conducted on the Internet.
Clinton had proposed to create a "free-trade zone" on the Internet. He wanted an agreement on this within a year within the context of the World Trade Organisation (WTO).
Rexrodt said he did not think the Internet should become a "global duty-free shop", but he was ready to discuss whether to abolish tariffs for cyberspace products and services.

The ministers also agreed that intermediaries like network operators and access providers should not in general be responsible for illegal content unless they had "reasonable grounds to know and reasonable possibility to control content".
The document was signed by a total of 29 countries, including all EU members, Eastern European nations and members of the European Free Trade Association.
The United States, Canada, Japan and Russia were observers at the conference and did not sign the final statement.
The main sticking point was how to regulate encryption technology that lets companies and individuals protect messages and transactions on the Internet by encoding them.

The United States heavily restricts export of encryption technology and requires companies to provide a so-called key that would allow law enforcement officials to "recover," or decode, encrypted messages.

"We feel very strongly that there must be a balance between encrypting products to protect them and legitimate law enforcement and security concerns," U.S. Commerce Secretary William Daley told a reporters at the conference.

While some companies say they must be free to develop and use their own encryption technology, some governments, like the U.S. and France, have said the state must be able to decipher such codes in case they are being used for criminal purposes.

"Our vision of electronic trade... will only become reality when users can be guaranteed absolute security of the transfer and processing of their data," Ron Sommer, chairman of Germany's Deutsche Telekom told the conference.

The ministers said they would consult industry on types of regulatory measures needed on the Internet rather than taking up the matter themselves, and said the so-called Bonn Declaration would provide a good framework for the future.

"We will use the declaration as a basis for what we are proposing in legislation," said European Commissioner Martin Bangemann. "But in terms of global regulation we lack competence. We need a global body to set principles and legislate accordingly," he said.
